implementation_notes: Nest's microservices layer owns the correlation: the server declares @MessagePattern(pattern) and the client calls ClientProxy.send(pattern, payload), which returns an Observable per request whose reply channel and correlation the transporter maintains - NATS gets an inbox subject for free, other transports get two logical channels that Nest wires up. Callers convert with lastValueFrom and bound the wait with the rxjs timeout operator, remembering that ClientProxy is lazy and connects on first use. Over WebSockets, socket.io's emitWithAck with ackTimeout is the same exchange with the acknowledgement as the reply channel.
pitfalls: The lazy ClientProxy establishes its connection on the first send, so that first request pays setup latency and can trip a short deadline; call connect() in onApplicationBootstrap.
rxjs timeout throws TimeoutError (an RxJS error) and unsubscribing cancels only local observation unless the transporter supports cancellation - convert both to domain errors at the boundary.
Log-based transporters such as Kafka are not request/reply at heart: Nest emulates the reply channel and a missing reply surfaces as an RxJS error, not a transport timeout.

variants.name: socket.io acknowledgement with ackTimeout
variants.implementation_notes: socket.io correlates a reply with its request without application code: passing an acknowledgement callback (or awaiting emitWithAck) makes the server's callback argument the reply channel, and the client's ackTimeout and retries options supply the deadline. Use it for browser-to-server request/reply; the exchange is tied to a live socket, so a disconnected client loses in-flight requests unless the application adds request ids and retry/idempotency.
pitfalls: ackTimeout rejects the promise but the server may still run the handler and emit an ack nobody reads: carry a request id and deduplicate on the server.
Browser sockets reconnect with backoff and buffer emits by default, so calls made while disconnected are delayed rather than failed.
